Anthropic announced Fable 5.1 at a price of $10 / $50 / $0.25 , which, in addition to having strictly better benchmark performance in all areas than Fable 5 from June at $10 / $50 / $1 , cut the cache read cost by 75%.
When using agents for coding, cache read costs are the vast majority (96% - 99%) of the total token expenditure as the cache is what contains the entire previous conversation each turn.
Additionally, the cache tends to be hit around 90 - 100% of the time (varies by the infrastructure of the LLM inference provider).
Taken together, a 75% reduction in the cache read cost correlates to a 70-75% reduction in the cost of using the model—obviously notable, even if cache costs are typically a footnote!
OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra, which is similar in size to Fable 5.1 and has similar pricing at $10 / $50 / $1 but without the lower cache read cost.
OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol at at a shocking price of $2 / $10 / $0.20 that halves the input and output price relative to the temporarily-discounted GPT-5.6 Sol!
They simultaneously released GPT-6 Luna also at half the input and output price ( $0.10 / $0.50 / $0.01 ) of the previous version.
On the same exact day , Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, where it’s explicitly stated “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that”.

Its price of $4 / $20 / $0.20 is much lower in total than Opus 5’s due to a 20% input/output cost cut and a larger cache read cut, resulting in a total cost reduction of 40-60% for a model that’s even better than Fable 5.1 (I have quite a lot of things to say about Opus 5.5, but that’s for another post).

It turned out that GPT-6 Sol was a dud performancewise, so a week later OpenAI announced GPT-6.1 Sol, which surprisingly has comparable performance to Astra (can confirm after personal use), but OpenAI casually cut the cache price in half ( $2 / $10 / $0.10 ) matching Anthropic’s 5%-of-input cache read cost, making this model family cumulatively 75% cheaper.
Data from Vercel’s AI model gateway supporting the decreasing cost-per-token trend to 43.3% of the April 2026 cost.

For open weight models, let’s take another look at DeepSeek Flash V4.1 , which also recently released an updated 1017 variant .

The original DeepSeek V4 Flash 0420 was released in April 2026 at a price of $0.14 / $0.28 / $0.0028 and went megaviral as a result, especially as OpenAI didn’t have a small-class model for simple tasks at the time.

That $0.0028 turned out to be the key, as a cache read proportion of 2% is substantially lower than the 5%-10% of the OpenAI and Anthropic models above, which makes the effective cost even lower than what is advertised.
I suspect the 80% GPT-5.6 Luna price cut in July was meant to specifically compete with these smaller open-weight models.

Now, the new DeepSeek Flash V4.1 1017 model performs significantly better than DeepSeek Flash V4 benchmark-wise ( 45 on the Artificial Analysis index vs. 24 ) and the cost from DeepSeek remains similar at $0.15 / $0.60 / $0.003 .
For the updated 1017 variant, there are now 29 distinct providers .
Effective costs by endpoint, with Cloudflare and DeepInfra within 10% of DeepSeek’s cost.

OpenAI and Anthropic will have to differentiate from these open weight models with higher-quality models—they are currently doing a good job with that particularly with Opus 5.5—but they need to keep doing that, which is why billions of dollars are being invested into R&D.

Open-weight models are catching up fast: just a few days ago, Moonshot AI announced Kimi K3.1 Pro which has comparable performance to Opus 5.5 (Kimi at 55 vs. Opus 5.5 at 58 ) at half the input/output price and the same cache read cost ( $2 / $10 / $0.20 ).

It’s the same size and architecture as Kimi K3 which is currently being hosted by over 20 distinct inference providers: once the weights drop on November 4th, you can therefore expect most of them to support the new Kimi K3.1 Pro model at a roughly equivalent price.
Notably, Moonshot AI itself is joining the price cut fun and priced Kimi K3.1 Pro at less than the original Kimi K3 ( $3 / $15 / $0.30 ).

The 29 distinct providers on OpenRouter have little incentive to serve an unprofitable model (they would just stop serving it and use the compute capacity for a profitable model instead) and “the true cost of a token” may end up being where price equals marginal cost.
So, why did they cut their primary revenue source by up to 80%?
The profit margins on inference themselves likely tell a different story, with some reports saying the profit-per-token margins are as healthy as 80% with caveats.

I used to have a $100/month subscription to Codex (the 5x Pro plan) when GPT-5.6 Sol was the top model, and I managed to just fully exhaust all the usage included in the subscription despite getting annoyed with random usage resets .
Once GPT-6.1 Sol released and I noticed that the cost of using it was effectively cut by 75%, you know what I did?

For example, at the same time GPT-6.1 Sol was announced, OpenAI cut the usage allowance by 50% for the $200/month tier in Codex under the argument “to reflect our increasingly efficient models”—which is technically correct but it’s funny to put in writing.
After Opus 5.5 released a month ago, there hasn’t been any discussion about either Fable 5.1 or GPT-6 Astra because Opus 5.5 is just that good.

Another less-cynical factor that could explain the price cuts is that LLM infrastructure has improved over the past few months—when Anthropic said “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that,” I believe it.
